title: Classroom words with a technical second sense

words.nuance: The only one here whose specialist sense is a **physical object you can point to** — the paragraph at the top of a paper — rather than a property of something else. It's also the only one that shifts stress to become a verb (ab-STRAKT, *to extract*). Watch for the trap that it means "vague": abstract is distance from the concrete, and can be perfectly exact.

Unique in the group for having two senses that pull in **opposite directions**: in a grammar or literature passage it means "don't take this at face value," but in a gallery it means the picture *does* show a real, recognisable thing — the direct antonym of abstract art. The surrounding subject, not the sentence, tells you which one is live.

The technical sense is a **grammatical category** — a word-form suffix that signals smallness or fondness (*piglet, kitchenette, Annie*), not a description of size at all. In its ordinary sense it lands almost exclusively on **people** and carries an appraising tilt, charmed or patronising depending on the speaker. Smallness of stature only; never of importance.

Here the everyday sense is the **noun** (a film) and the tested sense is the adjective — the reverse of the pattern in the rest of the group. In legal and historical prose it means *written record*: evidence you can put in a folder, opposed to **testimonial** evidence that walks in and talks. It stakes a quiet claim to reliability — paper can't misremember.

The one word in the group whose technical sense carries a built-in **downgrade**: it concedes nobody witnessed the thing, and the facts merely surround it. Pair it against documentary — record versus inference. Its older sense is a genuine reversal to watch for: a *circumstantial account* is one packed with detail, not one short of proof.

core: Each of these is a word you first met as a plain descriptive term, and each has a second life as a term of art inside one specific discipline — publishing, art criticism, linguistics, law, history. The GRE rarely wants the sense you learned in school; it drops the word into a passage where the specialist sense is the only one that fits and lets the familiar meaning mislead you. The tell is always the surrounding subject matter, not the sentence itself.
exam_note: The exam plants the everyday sense as a plausible-looking wrong answer and rewards the disciplinary one — so read the passage's field before you read the word.
